# Rewriting the Past in the Present: Ideology, Memory, Commemoration, and the Struggle for Historical Meaning

Historical narratives are being reinterpreted today because political and social actors use the past to answer present questions: who belongs to the nation, which institutions deserve legitimacy, whose suffering counts, and what forms of justice are possible. The central mechanisms are selection and omission, reframing and equivalence, sacralization and othering, and the institutionalization of preferred accounts through laws, curricula, museums, monuments, rituals, and digital media. These mechanisms can produce nationalist exclusion and historical coercion, but they can also expose silences and restore marginalized people as historical subjects.

The evidence also shows that no actor controls memory completely. States and political movements possess exceptional resources, yet activists, survivors, museums, historians, communities, material remains, and audiences can contest official accounts. Commemoration is therefore not simply the public display of historiography: it is one of the places where historiography is made, challenged, and redirected.

## Roadmap

The analysis first clarifies the difference between history, historical narrative, and collective memory, then distinguishes the broad ideological organization of the past from its more tactical instrumentalization. It next examines state and movement projects in Central and Eastern Europe, Russia and Ukraine, Germany, India, and the United States. The discussion then turns to efforts to reclaim silenced Indigenous, racialized, gendered, queer, subaltern, and colonial histories, before analyzing how monuments, museums, anniversaries, rituals, textbooks, and renaming controversies reshape public and academic history. The final sections compare these cases through the questions of identity, legitimacy, nationalism, reconciliation, justice, and political contestation, while distinguishing evidence about narrative production from evidence about public reception.

## 1. What It Means to Reinterpret History

### History, memory, and the present

A historical event and the narrative later constructed about it are related but not identical. The event leaves traces—documents, bodies, buildings, oral testimony, landscapes, legal records, and material remains—but those traces do not organize themselves into a universally accepted story. Historical narratives select, order, name, connect, and interpret them. The political significance of reinterpretation lies precisely in this relationship between what happened and what a society says happened.

Memory studies has challenged the idea that collective memory is a storehouse in which a group passively preserves a fixed past. Maurice Halbwachs’s concept of social frameworks emphasized that remembering takes place within institutions and social relationships. Pierre Nora’s account of *lieux de mémoire* drew attention to sites where memory becomes concentrated in monuments, museums, anniversaries, symbols, and rituals. Jan Assmann’s account of political memory similarly stresses mediation across generations through libraries, museums, monuments, education, and repeated occasions for collective participation. In the formulation summarized by a review of memory-politics scholarship, an affectively charged narrative turns history into political memory through “selecting and excluding” [the memory-politics review](https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/government-and-opposition/article/politics-of-memory-between-history-identity-and-conflict/DAB6FF02FBA7DEE05F92DE32FC833219).

This does not mean that historical claims are infinitely malleable. Michel-Rolph Trouillot rejects both the idea that people are prisoners of their pasts and the idea that history is simply whatever they choose to make of it. Historical knowledge remains constrained by evidence and materiality, even though access to evidence and the authority to interpret it are unequally distributed. His central point is that power enters historical production before a finished narrative appears, through the making of sources, the creation of archives, the retrieval of facts, and the production of retrospective significance [Trouillot, *Silencing the Past*](https://www.metodos.work/wp-content/uploads/2021/05/Michel-Rolph-Trouillot-Silencing-the-Past_-Power-and-the-Production-of-History-20th-Anniversary.pdf).

Trouillot’s example of the Alamo illustrates how narrative meaning can change without the underlying event changing. The defenders of the mission were defeated by Antonio López de Santa Anna’s forces on March 6, 1836. After Sam Houston defeated Santa Anna at San Jacinto on April 21, the cry “Remember the Alamo!” recast the earlier defeat as a heroic trial necessary to the later victory. The military event remained the same, but its place in the story changed: defeat became sacrifice, and sacrifice became evidence that victory was destined. Narrative reinterpretation therefore does not require the invention of new facts. It can operate by changing the plot into which established facts are inserted.

The same process can elevate one figure while silencing another. In the Haitian Revolution, Trouillot contrasts Henry Christophe, whose palace and monuments preserved his public significance, with Jean-Baptiste Sans Souci, an African-born commander whose military importance was documented but whose role was long treated as marginal. The palace named Sans Souci helped preserve the name while obscuring the man. This is not a simple absence of evidence. It is a pattern in which the surviving monument, the conventions of nationalist historiography, and the social status of different narrators direct attention toward one meaning and away from another.

### Where power enters the narrative

Trouillot’s four moments are useful because they show that silencing does not occur only when a historian deliberately suppresses information.

First, silences enter when sources are created. Some actions are recorded, while others leave no written trace; official records may classify people through the categories of the state; oral testimony may remain outside institutions that confer archival authority. Second, silences enter when archives assemble and organize sources. Archives decide which producers, documents, themes, and procedures become accessible and credible. Third, they enter when historians and public narrators retrieve some facts more often than others. Finally, they enter when societies decide which events possess lasting retrospective significance.

These moments overlap. A colonial administration may create records that classify Indigenous people through bureaucratic categories; an archive may preserve those records more systematically than Indigenous testimony; historians may then treat the official archive as the central source of knowledge; and a national museum may transform the resulting narrative into a public origin story. Later activism can challenge each stage by recovering oral histories, demanding access to archives, changing the terminology of public institutions, or creating new commemorative sites.

The reinterpretation of history is therefore not only a dispute over “facts.” It is also a dispute over who can produce facts, which forms of evidence are recognized, which categories are treated as natural, and which audiences are assumed to matter. The 1992 Columbian quincentennial demonstrated this clearly. “Discovery” presents the event from the standpoint of European arrival, whereas “conquest” foregrounds invasion and domination. Trouillot argues that naming is already an interpretive act: a society that calls the landing a discovery has placed Europe at the center of the historical field before explaining what happened to the people who were already there. The difference between “discovery,” “encounter,” and “conquest” is not merely semantic; each term organizes political responsibility differently [Trouillot, *Silencing the Past*](https://www.metodos.work/wp-content/uploads/2021/05/Michel-Rolph-Trouillot-Silencing-the-Past_-Power-and-the-Production-of-History-20th-Anniversary.pdf).

### Ideologisation and instrumentalisation

Two concepts help distinguish different kinds of political use.

| Dimension | Ideologisation of history | Instrumentalisation of the past |
|---|---|---|
| Scope | Organizes many episodes into a coherent worldview | Mobilizes a selected event, symbol, grievance, or victim identity |
| Typical question | Who are “we,” and who belongs outside the community? | What political objective can this past help achieve now? |
| Main operations | Selection, omission, equivalence, othering, sacralization, institutionalization | Timing, amplification, legal action, electoral framing, symbolic performance |
| Main media | Curricula, museums, research institutes, laws, national rituals | Campaigns, speeches, commemorative actions, reparations claims, wartime rhetoric |
| Typical risk | Closure of pluralism and exclusion of inconvenient histories | Tactical escalation, scapegoating, or reduction of complex history to a usable slogan |

The distinction is analytical rather than absolute. A broad ideology supplies the worldview within which a particular event becomes useful, while a tactical use can reinforce the ideology that made it possible. Russia’s Great Patriotic War memory is an ideological foundation of state identity and also a strategic resource in wartime rhetoric. Poland’s narrative of national innocence is part of a wider nationalist history and was also mobilized through a specific Holocaust law. Hindutva’s account of an ancient Hindu civilization interrupted by Muslim rule is an ideological worldview, while Ayodhya converts that worldview into a concrete political claim over land, citizenship, and national sovereignty.

Bucholc distinguishes “memory politics,” which manages and controls the contents of collective memory, from “historical politics,” which advocates a particular vision of the past as historical narrative. Historical politics can therefore be part of the broader field of memory politics [Bucholc on memory and historical politics](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40803-018-0080-7). Erik Meyer’s related distinction separates *policy for the past*—legal measures, amnesties, institutional arrangements, and other practical responses—from *politics of history*, which seeks cultural hegemony through symbolic communication. This distinction helps explain why a government may use history both to make policy and to shape the interpretive environment in which policy appears legitimate [the memory-politics review](https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/government-and-opposition/article/politics-of-memory-between-history-identity-and-conflict/DAB6FF02FBA7DEE05F92DE32FC833219).

A further debate concerns motive. Instrumentalist accounts emphasize political manipulation by elites. Cultural and constructivist accounts stress that leaders operate within existing memories, institutions, identities, and social expectations. Thomas Berger’s framework distinguishes historical determinism, instrumentalism, and cultural explanation, while Jennifer Dixon’s work, as summarized in the review literature, argues that international pressure increases the likelihood that official narratives will change but domestic factors shape what those changes contain. Narrative revision is therefore neither pure manipulation nor automatic cultural inheritance. It emerges through interaction among political actors, institutions, social groups, and external pressures.

## 2. Ideologisation of History

Ideologisation occurs when historical interpretation becomes a comprehensive account of collective identity and political order. It does not merely say that an event happened in a certain way. It establishes a moral geography: victims and perpetrators, founders and outsiders, authentic citizens and alleged traitors, civilized actors and barbaric enemies. Its characteristic effect is to make a current political arrangement appear to be the continuation, restoration, or defense of an older order.

### Anticommunism and the politics of post-communist Europe

Central and Eastern Europe provides a particularly clear example because post-1989 states had to decide how to interpret communism, fascism, national collaboration, resistance, and the Soviet role in the defeat of Nazi Germany. These were not only scholarly questions. They affected lustration, the legitimacy of successor parties, relations with Russia, European integration, and the definition of national victimhood.

Zuzana Dujisin describes the post-communist development of state-sponsored memory institutes as the emergence of a transnational field of anticommunism. The institutes were created partly because conservative actors regarded direct lustration and prosecution as politically difficult or ineffective. Research, archival control, and public education appeared to offer a more durable way to establish the “true” history of communism. The resulting institutions occupied an intermediate space between political parties and historiography: they could present a partisan historical project in the language of professional research and public education [Dujisin, “A history of post-communist remembrance”](https://doi.org/10.1007/s11186-020-09401-5).

The Polish Institute of National Remembrance illustrates this arrangement. Established in 1998, it inherited archives and infrastructure and was given responsibilities that included research, public education, and the investigation of communist and Nazi crimes. Its supporters saw it as a way to complete an “unfinished revolution” by confronting former communist networks. Critics feared that it would turn historical research and archival access into instruments of political revenge. Under Janusz Kurtyka, the institute’s educational and research activities expanded, while historians linked to the Law and Justice Party gained influence.

The Hungarian Terror House Museum developed a different but related narrative. Housed in a building associated first with Hungarian fascists and then with the communist secret police, it presents fascism and communism through a shared architecture of terror. Yet the museum devotes almost all of its rooms to communism, and its “wall of perpetrators” links former communist officials to the families and political networks of contemporary liberal politicians. The museum thus converts a history of dictatorship into a contemporary political map. Its large opening audience and school visits gave the narrative a public ritual form rather than leaving it within academic debate.

These institutions cannot be reduced to propaganda outlets. They provided archives, exhibitions, teacher training, and research opportunities that addressed genuinely suppressed or neglected experiences. Some Polish Institute of National Remembrance historians also investigated Polish participation in the Holocaust, contradicting the idea that an anticommunist institution could produce only national self-exoneration. Yet the institutional structure made pluralism vulnerable: an institute created to establish a morally unified national history could support critical research in one field while suppressing it in another.

The Europeanization of this project added a transnational layer. In 2008, the European Parliament established August 23 as a day of remembrance for the victims of Stalinism and Nazism. In 2009, it called for cooperation among national research institutes specializing in totalitarian history. Between 2012 and 2016, the Platform of European Memory and Conscience circulated an exhibition on “Fascism—Nazism—Communism” through museums, memorials, universities, parliaments, and cultural centers in 15 European countries. Its structure alternated Nazi and communist crimes and suggested a historical connection between the two systems [Dujisin, “A history of post-communist remembrance”](https://doi.org/10.1007/s11186-020-09401-5).

The narrative met different needs. For many Central and Eastern European actors, Western Europe’s Holocaust-centered memory appeared to neglect their experience of Soviet domination. The comparison could therefore function as a demand for recognition. But critics warned that equating Nazism and communism could create false equivalence, obscure local collaboration, and transform national victimhood into a means of avoiding responsibility. Jelena Subotić argues that post-communist states have appropriated Holocaust memory to highlight other suffering, reject communism, and imagine a pre-communist ethnically pure nation. Ljiljana Radonić similarly warns that the Holocaust template and the language of genocide can rationalize radical policies and deflect blame for present domestic failures.

The disagreement is not simply between “Western” and “Eastern” memory. It concerns what comparison does. Comparison can widen the field of recognized suffering, but it can also flatten differences in historical context and political responsibility. A plural history of dictatorship need not require a hierarchy of suffering; conversely, recognition of Eastern European victims need not entail an ideological equivalence between Nazi racial extermination and Soviet communism. The political stakes arise when a comparative frame becomes a legal or institutional requirement for belonging to the nation.

### Poland: national innocence and the limits of pluralism

Poland’s memory politics shows how ideologisation can operate through institutions, curricula, public space, and law at the same time. Under the Law and Justice government from 2015 to 2023, historical policy was fused with state objectives. Museums, research institutes, school curricula, academic publication systems, public funding, and street names were revised to promote a narrative of Polish suffering, rescue, resistance, and anti-communism. The narrative resisted emphasis on Polish hostility or indifference toward Jews, Ukrainians, Belarusians, Lemkos, Silesians, and Roma [Wójcik on Polish memory laws](https://doi.org/10.53483/xcnv3562).

The debate over Jedwabne exposed the conflict. In 2000, Jan T. Gross’s *Neighbours* documented the murder of several hundred Jews by Polish neighbors in July 1941. President Aleksander Kwaśniewski apologized in 2001. Yet Jarosław Kaczyński used the controversy electorally to claim that Poland’s enemies were turning Poles into “Hitler’s associates.” The same event thus supported two rival national projects: a self-critical account that made responsibility part of citizenship, and a defensive account that represented the accusation itself as an attack on the nation.

The Polish Centre for Holocaust Research’s *Night without an End* deepened the challenge. Its micro-historical studies of nine districts found that at least 60 percent of Jews who survived the deadliest phase of the Holocaust in those districts were denounced or killed by Christian neighbors. An extrapolation from the nine districts suggested approximately 200,000 deaths nationally, but the source explicitly treats that number as a projection rather than a nationwide count. The research prompted pressure on Barbara Engelking, Jan Grabowski, the Centre’s journal, and associated museums. At the same time, new institutions such as the Ulma Family Museum and the Chapel of Memory of Rescuers promoted a parallel narrative of Polish rescue and self-sacrifice [Kończal on the Polish Holocaust Law](https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/european-review/article/mnemonic-populism-the-polish-holocaust-law-and-its-afterlife/7A5CB69785AF057A849ABED824FEBD4E).

This institutional conflict demonstrates that ideologisation does not always suppress a fact directly. It can instead alter the relative visibility of competing facts. Rescue stories become central, while collaboration becomes exceptional; Polish victimhood is placed beside Jewish victimhood in a way that can imply moral equivalence; a museum’s spatial design can make one version emotionally immediate and another appear marginal.

### Holocaust remembrance, European identity, and competing memories

Germany provides a different form of ideological memory politics. The Federal Republic’s remembrance of National Socialism has often been described as a “negative founding myth”: legal prohibitions on Holocaust denial and Nazi symbols, memorial sites, museums, and public rituals establish the rejection of Nazism as a basis of democratic legitimacy. This memory regime has supported public responsibility and constrained nationalist rehabilitation. It cannot simply be treated as equivalent to the self-exculpatory memory politics found elsewhere.

Yet it remains selective. Stenlund argues that the contemporary European Union uses the Holocaust as a moral and historical point of departure for European values, human-rights legislation, and the authority of European law. The author contrasts this official narrative with the 1951 Treaty of Paris, whose preamble emphasized economic development and world peace without explicitly invoking the genocide of European Jews or human-rights protection through law. The argument is not that European integration was unrelated to Nazi crimes, but that its historical self-description has changed as present institutional needs have changed [Stenlund on European Holocaust memory](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10978-025-09420-0).

This change is visible at Auschwitz. The museum’s national exhibitions opened in the 1960s in state-socialist Poland. Their emphasis moved from collection and preservation to socialism as an interpretive frame and, later, to human rights. People outside the socialist bloc gained broader access after the fall of the Berlin Wall. The site therefore does not possess one timeless meaning; its interpretation has been repeatedly reorganized in response to different political cultures.

Michael Rothberg’s account of Germany’s “Historikerstreit 2.0” makes the tension more explicit. The 1986 Historians’ Debate concerned attempts by conservative historians to relativize Nazi crimes by comparing them with Stalinist crimes. The debates of 2020–2021 instead connected Holocaust memory to German colonialism, migration, racism, antisemitism, and the crisis in Israel and Palestine. Rothberg argues that Germany’s dominant Holocaust memory regime, while a major achievement of the 1980s and 1990s, has reached limits in a postmigrant society. He advocates attention to multidirectional memory, in which different histories of violence can enter relation without being collapsed into equivalence [Rothberg on “Historikerstreit 2.0”](https://doi.org/10.1177/17506980221133511).

Stenlund similarly notes that colonial atrocities and Sami memories remain marginal within the official European Holocaust-centered narrative. Here the issue is not whether the Holocaust should be remembered, but whether its institutional centrality permits other histories to be heard. The danger is twofold: attempts to displace Holocaust memory can become revisionist, while an absolute uniqueness regime can make colonial, Indigenous, migrant, or racialized histories appear politically threatening rather than historically connected.

### Russia and Ukraine: competing master narratives

Russia and Ukraine demonstrate how similar institutional techniques can serve opposing ideological projects. Since the 1990s, both states have used centralized education, dominant public discourse, memory laws, and administrative regulation to create political cohesion. Russia introduced a single cultural standard for school history in 2013. Ukraine established a unified history curriculum after independence and, after 2014, intensified decommunization and the legal regulation of public memory [Kasianov on Russian-Ukrainian historical politics](https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/nationalities-papers/article/history-politics-in-the-russian-ukrainian-relations-the-2000s2022-shared-past-as-a-casus-belli/24B5F059988F2EE9BC8D97EB67FEA4CA).

The similarity of methods must not obscure the asymmetry of political projects. Russia’s narrative increasingly revived imperial nationalism, a unique Russian path, and the idea that Russians and Ukrainians constitute one historical people. Ukraine’s narrative emphasized sovereignty, national emancipation, and separation from Russian domination. The same shared past therefore became, for Russia, an argument for reintegration and, for Ukraine, a starting point for independence.

The legal consequences were also unequal in scale. In Russia, more than 6,000 citizens were summoned to court under the 2014 memory law between 2014 and 2019, with approximately two-thirds receiving administrative fines according to the source summarized by Kasianov. The designation of Memorial as a “foreign agent” effectively made its work impossible. In Ukraine, 119 cases were opened between 2014 and 2019, mostly concerning public use of Soviet and communist symbols; after February 2022, approximately 200 cases under the decommunization law ended in sentences. The figures demonstrate coercive institutionalization, but they do not by themselves establish how ordinary citizens interpreted the laws or whether the resulting narratives became socially persuasive.

The conflict became more than a dispute over curriculum. Russia’s official rationale for the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022 relied on quasi-historical arguments that denied Ukraine’s independent historical subjectivity. Ukrainian actors framed the war as a continuation of resistance to Russian imperialism. The past became securitized: rival historical narratives were treated as threats to the existence of the national self. Nekoliak describes Russian memory laws as enshrining state-approved interpretations and argues that Russia’s militant memory politics denied Ukraine’s mnemonic sovereignty [Nekoliak on memory laws in Russia and Ukraine](https://memocracy.eu/static/1ab0423ed274d09d26f038f5ae9b6f3b/Nekoliak_Memory-Laws-in-Russia-and-Ukraine-final.pdf).

### Hindutva, school history, and ideological selection

India provides a major example of ideologisation through school curricula and national mythology. Anand and Lall’s review of textbook politics from 1998 to 2020 finds a clear relationship between changes in governing parties and changes in the schoolbooks used. During the BJP government of 1998–2004, the National Curriculum Framework of 2000 adopted the premise of “Indianise, nationalise and spiritualise.” The framework was criticized for treating Muslims as perpetual aggressors and for removing or marginalizing cultural elements associated with Islamic rule [Anand and Lall on Indian textbooks](https://discovery.ucl.ac.uk/id/eprint/10148572/1/The%20debate%20between%20secularism%20and%20Hindu%20nationalism%20how%20India%20s%20textbooks%20have%20become%20the%20government%20s%20medium%20for%20political%20communication.pdf).

After 2014, the process acquired greater scale and centralization. Parandhama identifies three connected changes: affective framing, centralized curricular control, and epistemic substitution. In this account, contestable social history and parts of the scientific curriculum are displaced by mythic narratives and claims of indigenous knowledge. The analysis reports that NCERT revisions in 2023 removed or truncated sections on the Mughal Empire and the Delhi Sultanate, shortened passages from chronicles such as the *Akbarnama* and *Badshah Nama*, muted discussion of the 2002 Gujarat violence, and removed contextual details about Gandhi’s assassination. NCERT officials attributed the changes to workload rationalization after the COVID-19 pandemic, while critics connected them to Hindu-nationalist politics; the competing explanations should be kept distinct [Parandhama on Indian curriculum politics](https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/political-science/articles/10.3389/fpos.2025.1731252/full).

A content analysis by Patil found that changing the textbook theme from the singular “our past” to the plural “our pasts” in 2005 did not substantially change the content. Dalit, Dalit-women, and tribal histories continued to appear as “other” rather than as central components of the national story [Patil on caste and gender in NCERT history](https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/2455632719880622).

The ideological pattern extends beyond curriculum. Truschke argues that Hindutva narratives construct an imagined Hindu golden age interrupted by Muslim invaders and use that story to make modern Hindu nationalism appear ancient and Muslims appear as the ultimate Other. The Ayodhya temple project became a material expression of this narrative: in 1992, a Hindu mob illegally demolished a premodern mosque, after which violence across northern India killed a few thousand people, mainly Muslims; in August 2020, Hindu nationalist groups celebrated the ground-breaking of a Ram temple on the site [Truschke on Hindutva historical narratives](https://journals.openedition.org/samaj/6636).

In the United States, ideological selection has also occurred through state education laws, although the institutional structure is different. A 2023 analysis reported that Republican state legislatures in more than half of the 50 states had proposed or passed measures restricting teaching about race, sex, bias, or the contributions of minority groups to American history. Florida’s 2022 law restricted instruction that could make students or employees feel guilt for historical events committed by members of their race, or that represented races or sexes as privileged or oppressed. The article interpreted these laws as substituting a nationalist, Christian, and white-centered account for narratives emphasizing systemic racism and sexism, while also noting that the laws codified longstanding exclusions from school history [analysis of contemporary U.S. history education](https://www.redalyc.org/journal/6720/672074280002/html/).

The comparison with India should not erase institutional differences. India’s curriculum revisions were connected to national educational institutions and a centralized Hindu-nationalist project; the United States case involves state-level conflict within a federal system and competing claims about parental authority, academic freedom, and psychological harm. The common mechanism is the use of education to define which historical categories are legitimate and which forms of inequality may be named.

## 3. Instrumentalisation of the Past

Ideologisation establishes a worldview; instrumentalisation makes a selected element of the past do immediate political work. The past may be used to mobilize voters, defend a territory, criminalize speech, justify a war, legitimate a constitutional change, or turn a grievance into a claim for compensation. The use is not necessarily insincere. Actors may genuinely believe the historical claim while also recognizing its strategic value.

### Russia’s war memory as political action

The Great Patriotic War is the central resource of Russian state-sponsored memory. It refers specifically to the period from Nazi Germany’s attack on the Soviet Union on June 22, 1941, to the German surrender on May 9, 1945, Moscow time. Since 2014, its memory has been connected to military reenactments, commemorative marches, portraits of fallen relatives, decorated cars, and narratives in which Russian speakers in Donetsk and Luhansk appear as victims and Russian soldiers as heroic saviors [the temporality of memory politics](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11890424/).

The strategic power of the narrative lies in continuity. If the war against Ukraine is presented as a continuation of the fight against fascism, then present military action becomes defense rather than aggression, and political opposition can be cast as betrayal. Russian state media shifted after the 2013 Euromaidan protests from describing Ukrainians as a “brotherly nation,” albeit within a hierarchical imperial frame, to constructing Ukrainians as Russia’s main “Other.” The study of this narrative links it to the justification of the occupation of Crimea in 2014 and later military aggression, while cautioning that its media analysis does not measure audience reception.

A 2025 study of 5,166 Ukraine-related documents from Russian state-backed coverage between August 2021 and August 2022 coded a random sample of 516 articles. It identifies a movement from “historicism,” in which the past is represented as a distinct period, toward “mythic time,” in which past and present collapse. As the reflective distance between past and present disappears, appeals shift from evaluating historical evidence toward identity and patriotic agitation. The study analyzes narrative construction, not the persuasive effect of the coverage [the temporality of memory politics](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11890424/).

Other research demonstrates how the war memory is sacralized. An analysis of ten Vladimir Putin speeches published in 2022 and 2023, totaling more than 43,000 words, identifies religious imagery, sacred historical myths, heroic and sacrificial community, exceptionalism, moral duty, and existential dichotomy as recurring techniques. Crimea is presented as a sacred and civilizational space, associated with the baptism of Prince Vladimir and described as the spiritual source of the Russian nation and centralized state. Sacralization removes territory from ordinary political contestation: if land is part of national sacred identity, compromise can appear as desecration [analysis of sacralization in Russian official rhetoric](https://doi.org/10.1080/13569775.2024.2387436).

The same logic appeared in Russia’s 2020 constitutional amendments. References to ancestors, faith in God, and a man-woman definition of marriage accompanied provisions permitting two additional presidential terms for Vladimir Putin. The study argues that conservative historical and moral themes helped fill the political agenda and direct attention away from the expansion of presidential power. This is an interpretation of political function, not proof that all voters accepted the intended connection.

Commemorative actions carry the narrative beyond official speeches. A 2026 study of 156 Victory Volunteers press releases from 2022 to 2024 analyzes the annual St George’s Ribbon campaign as a state-directed practice. The ribbon, originally a World War II symbol, is presented as a means of preserving “historical truth” and supporting the idea that war is a normal and necessary condition of Russian existence. The group reported more than one million members across 89 regions in April 2026, though the authors caution that figures and website statements come from the organization itself and may not represent every member’s views [Mathers and Edwards on Victory Volunteers](https://researchspace.bathspa.ac.uk/17888/1/17888.pdf).

The circulation of war memory is not wholly top-down. A study of almost 300 state-aligned Russian-language Telegram channels in 2023 followed the movement of the term “Stalingrad” through news services, military bloggers, and prominent propagandists. The authors argue that repeated recontextualization made Stalingrad lose its historical distance and saturate the present feed, entangling World War II with the war against Ukraine. They call this condition “ambient war,” emphasizing repetition, rhythm, and availability rather than a single centrally authored message [Garner and Garner on Stalingrad in Telegram networks](https://doi.org/10.1177/17506352261477309).

Audience reception complicates the instrumentalist picture. An interview study combining 24 interviews conducted by the authors with 213 interviews from the Public Sociology Laboratory found that Russian citizens interpreted state war narratives in different ways: alignment, ambivalence, identity separation, or rejection. Seventy-five percent of the 24 author-interview respondents said they perceived an attempt to connect patriotism to the war, but recognition of the message did not entail acceptance. The study also links the reframing of Ukrainians from a “brother nation” to an enemy with a rise in negative views of Ukrainians among Russians from 17 percent before 2014 to 59 percent after the Euromaidan crisis, while cautioning that surveys conducted under authoritarian conditions may not fully reflect private attitudes [interview study of Russian narrative reception](https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/european-journal-of-international-security/article/identity-under-narrative-pressure-how-russian-citizens-navigate-strategic-war-narratives/239DB6E1565B979FA75E4F17E86BAE91).

A separate survey experiment found that no more than 5 percent of respondents wanted controversial historical topics entirely excluded from free-speech protections. Forty percent and a half said free speech should always include discussion of controversial history, while 54 percent favored some non-universal limits. Respondents were more punitive toward a controversial statement posted on social media than toward the same statement made in a classroom or bar, and criticism from a foreign academic was less tolerated than criticism from a Russian in-group member [survey experiment on historical dissent in Russia](https://doi.org/10.1017/s1537592722004169). These results show that state narratives create pressure without producing uniform belief.

### Poland: law, innocence, and electoral grievance

Poland’s 2018 Holocaust law illustrates a more direct form of strategic use. On January 26, 2018, Parliament adopted provisions making public claims that the Polish nation or state bore responsibility or co-responsibility for Nazi crimes punishable by a fine or up to three years’ imprisonment. International pressure led to the removal of criminal liability in June 2018, leaving the matter to civil courts. The law’s supporters presented it as a defense of national dignity and historical truth; critics saw it as an anti-pluralist attempt to define permissible historical attribution [Kończal on mnemonic populism](https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/european-review/article/mnemonic-populism-the-polish-holocaust-law-and-its-afterlife/7A5CB69785AF057A849ABED824FEBD4E).

The law’s political value lay in its ability to convert historical responsibility into present moral authority. If Poland is represented only as a victim and rescuer, criticism becomes foreign hostility. If Polish participation in persecution is admitted, national belonging can be defined through responsibility and historical self-examination. The law was therefore not simply about the wording of history; it was about who could speak, who could accuse, and which national identity the state would defend.

Reparations demands show how historical grievance can be used electorally without requiring a new academic interpretation. The PiS government presented Germany with official demands for €1.03 trillion in reparations for crimes committed during the Second World War. The communist government had renounced reparations claims in 1953, though the validity of that renunciation has been disputed by some scholars and politicians. In election campaigns, PiS portrayed opposition parties as “pro-German” and “anti-Polish”; opposition parties supported reparations but extended claims to Russia as the successor to the Soviet Union [Wójcik on Polish reparations politics](https://doi.org/10.53483/xcnv3562).

The historical claim can be sincere and strategic at the same time. It expresses real mass suffering and a disputed legal history, while also dividing the political field into patriots and alleged collaborators. Instrumentalisation does not require that the past be fabricated. It requires that one interpretation be selected because it performs a useful political function now.

### India: Ayodhya and the mobilization of grievance

The Ayodhya narrative demonstrates how a historical claim becomes a political instrument through a combination of sacred symbolism, legal dispute, mass mobilization, and public violence. The temple to the Hindutva version of Ram is presented not merely as a religious building but as the restoration of a civilizational truth. The mosque demolished in 1992 becomes evidence of Muslim domination and the temple becomes a sign of Hindu sovereignty. The political value of the past lies in its ability to turn a contested site into a test of national belonging.

Truschke’s analysis emphasizes that this narrative does not simply retrieve a premodern conflict. It constructs a modern identity by selectively arranging historical periods: Hindu rule is idealized, Muslim rule is demonized, and British colonialism receives less attention because it is less useful to contemporary Hindutva politics. The historical grievance therefore works prospectively. It defines the nation that political actors seek to build.

The same logic appears in textbook revision. Omitting or reducing the Mughal period, the Gujarat violence, or contextual information about Gandhi’s assassination does not by itself prove what students will believe. Anand and Lall explicitly caution that textbooks show what the state intends students to learn, not necessarily what they actually learn. But curricular selection still matters because it determines which historical questions children encounter as normal, controversial, or unmentionable.

### Europe and the United States: history as legal authority

Stenlund’s analysis of European Holocaust memory identifies another form of instrumentalisation: the use of a moral past to authorize present legal power. When the Holocaust is presented as the foundational reason for European unity, remembrance supports legislation against hate speech and strengthens the authority of European institutions. The author contrasts this with the earlier economic and peace-oriented language of the Treaty of Paris, arguing that the European historical narrative has been adapted to contemporary constitutional needs [Stenlund on European memory and law](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10978-025-09420-0).

The 2022 United States Supreme Court decision in *Dobbs v. Jackson Women’s Health Organization* provides a different example of history functioning as legal authority. According to a 2023 historical analysis, the majority treated state regulation of abortion when the Fourteenth Amendment was adopted in 1868 as the decisive historical reference. The dissent emphasized that constitutional rights were framed at a level of generality capable of adapting to changed social facts and law. The Organization of American Historians and American Historical Association criticized the majority’s historical evidence and argument, according to the article. The case demonstrates that “original history” is not merely retrieved; it is selected as the relevant level of historical meaning [analysis of history and *Dobbs*](https://www.redalyc.org/journal/6720/672074280002/html/).

The same article interprets the January 6 Select Committee as using historical documentation to establish legal and moral accountability for the attempt to overturn the 2020 presidential election. It also warns that an individual-centered narrative can leave institutional structures—such as electoral rules, money, media, and representation—untouched. Here history serves democratic accountability, but the choice of scale determines whether responsibility is assigned only to actors or also to systems.

These examples show why the political use of history cannot be assessed solely by asking whether a claim is “political.” All public history is situated in political worlds. The more precise questions are: what evidence is selected, what alternatives are excluded, which institutions gain authority, and whether the narrative expands or narrows the range of present action.

## 4. Reclaiming Silenced and Marginalized Narratives

Reclaiming a silenced narrative is not simply adding an omitted name to an existing story. It can involve changing the archive, redefining who counts as a historical subject, questioning the categories through which evidence was produced, and altering the spaces where the past is publicly encountered.

### Counter-memory and the politics of historical subjecthood

Trouillot’s account is valuable because it avoids treating silence as mere ignorance. Silencing is active and relational: a mention of one event can make another less visible; an archive can establish authority for one group’s testimony and doubt another’s; a monument can preserve a name while erasing the political conflict surrounding it. Reclamation therefore requires more than empirical enlargement. It may require changing the narrative structure that determines what counts as significant.

Hazel Carby’s foreword to *Silencing the Past* describes this work as repositioning scant evidence to generate new narratives and making silences speak against inequalities in sources, archives, and historical interpretation. The aim is not to replace one closed national story with another. It is to expose the power relations through which a story became dominant [Carby’s foreword to *Silencing the Past*](https://www.metodos.work/wp-content/uploads/2021/05/Michel-Rolph-Trouillot-Silencing-the-Past_-Power-and-the-Production-of-History-20th-Anniversary.pdf).

The recovery of a silenced narrative can itself reproduce exclusions. A national movement may recover its own suffering while continuing to marginalize minorities within the nation. This is visible in Ukraine, Poland, India, and South Africa, where counter-memory has challenged an imperial or official story but has not always produced a fully plural account.

### Ukraine’s Likbez and the limits of national recovery

In 2015, Ukrainian historian Kyrylo Halushko and colleagues launched *Likbez: History without Censorship* as a volunteer response to war and historical propaganda. The project published ten volumes between 2015 and 2016, covering Ukrainian territories from the Middle Ages to the mid-twentieth century. More than two dozen historians participated; thousands of copies of each volume were sold and distributed across Ukraine, alongside lectures and public discussions [review of Likbez](https://doi.org/10.1017/s0960777317000431).

Likbez challenged older Ukrainian and Soviet histories by bringing different imperial histories into a single narrative and presenting Ukraine as historically multinational. Its account of Crimea challenged the dominant Russian emphasis on rule from 1783 to 1954 by stressing centuries outside Russia and identifying Crimean Tatars as the peninsula’s only autochthonous population. It connected the violent Russification of the peninsula and Stalin’s 1944 deportation of all Crimean Tatars to the contemporary opposition to Russia’s 2014 annexation.

Yet the project also revealed the difficulty of turning national recovery into inclusive history. In its discussion of Galicia, Poles and Jews—who formed a large part of the region’s population until the Second World War—received little or no voice. The project varied in quality, lacked consistent footnotes, and relied largely on existing secondary research. It succeeded as public history and civic intervention, but it did not eliminate national bias from the narrative it sought to pluralize.

The case illustrates a recurrent pattern. Counter-memory can contest imperial erasure while still organizing the past around a titular nation. A narrative can be emancipatory relative to one power structure and exclusionary relative to another. The question is not whether a community has the right to remember its own oppression, but whether its public history can acknowledge the multiple communities that inhabited the same historical space.

### Indigenous truth-telling and digital heritage

Indigenous reclamation often challenges not only the content of national history but also the institutions and epistemologies through which history is produced. In Australia, Indigenous advocacy and cultural institutions, combined with digital technologies, have since the late 1990s enabled First Nations control over photographic and archival heritage. The Aṟa Irititja and Storylines projects allow communities to manage, circulate, contextualize, and sometimes restrict access to materials that were previously held by museums and state institutions [Lydon on Indigenous digital heritage](https://doi.org/10.1080/17514517.2021.1927369).

Projects such as Mukurtu CMS and Local Contexts make this principle operational. Mukurtu is designed to let communities manage and share digital heritage according to culturally relevant protocols. Local Contexts uses “TK Labels” to attach community-specific knowledge and access rules to heritage materials. These systems challenge the assumption that digitization automatically makes a collection public and that institutions should have unilateral authority to define its meaning.

Digital control does not solve structural inequality. Lydon notes continuing cultural loss, globalization, and unequal access. The importance of these projects lies less in technological novelty than in shifting the location of authority: Indigenous communities become producers and custodians of history rather than merely subjects represented by others.

Truth-telling extends this challenge into national politics. In Victoria, Australia, truth-telling has become part of efforts to imagine Indigenous emancipation and transform Indigenous-settler relations. Maddison, Hurst, and Thomas identify two competing scholarly perspectives. A normative account treats truth-telling as flawed but potentially transformative; a critical account warns that it can rehabilitate the settler-colonial state while leaving ongoing colonial structures intact [Maddison, Hurst, and Thomas on Australian truth-telling](https://doi.org/10.17645/si.v11i2.6491).

The tension is crucial. A state may acknowledge past violence in a way that strengthens Indigenous claims to justice, or it may convert acknowledgment into evidence that the state has already repaired its relationship with Indigenous peoples. Truth-telling becomes politically meaningful only if it changes the distribution of authority, land, resources, archival control, or institutional accountability. A ceremony of recognition alone does not establish that transformation.

Canada offers a more institutionalized model. In September 2020, the federal government designated the residential-school system an event of national historic significance and two former school buildings as national historic sites. Pentland places these designations within an official narrative containing more than 2,150 certified places, people, and events, most of which celebrate imperial history and silence Indigenous peoples. Residential-school commemoration can therefore disrupt a long-standing national narrative by honoring victims rather than imperial achievement [Pentland on Canadian commemoration](https://doi.org/10.33137/ijournal.v6i2.36456).

A 2025 comparative study finds that Canada has built truth-telling into legislation, permanent national institutions, and civic commemoration, while Australia’s initiatives remain uneven across jurisdictions, politically contingent, and insufficiently anchored in national law. The study concludes that truth-telling is unlikely to achieve transformative potential without durable frameworks, Indigenous governance, accountability, and implementation of the United Nations Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples [comparative study of Canada and Australia](https://research.monash.edu/en/publications/legislating-truth-comparative-lessons-from-canadas-national-truth/).

Canada’s institutionalization has advantages—continuity, visibility, and national responsibility—but it also creates risks. A government may define truth-telling through administrative procedures that contain its political implications. Australia’s fragmentation can weaken implementation, yet it may also leave greater room for locally specific Indigenous initiatives. Neither model guarantees justice; the comparison shows that institutional durability and Indigenous control are related but not identical.

### South Africa: reconciliation, structural violence, and public history

South Africa’s Truth and Reconciliation Commission demonstrates the ambiguous relationship between memory, justice, and national reconstruction. The Commission brought testimony about political violence into public view, but historians were largely absent from its process. Verbuyst’s review finds a divided historiographical response: some historians praise the Commission’s alternative engagement with the past, while many criticize its epistemology, ethics, methodology, and content. Others warn that its emphasis on a post-apartheid present can obscure unresolved structural violence [Verbuyst on the TRC and historiography](https://doi.org/10.4102/nc.v66i0.306).

The Commission’s archival afterlife was also constrained. Inaccessible archives prevented historians from fully following the historical roadmap implied by its work. Some nevertheless used the Commission as a stimulus for oral-history projects and public history. This is a key distinction: a truth commission may generate testimony without automatically generating a usable historical archive.

Grunebaum argues that the TRC’s nation-building project mediated individual testimonies into a homogeneous collective narrative. Its founding terms focused primarily on political violence between the apartheid state and liberation movements, leaving racialized structural and administrative violence less visible. Forced displacement was a major example. Research published in 1985 estimated that more than 3.5 million people were forcibly displaced in South Africa between 1960 and the mid-1980s, yet 1990s public debates around the TRC largely overlooked the right of return, restitution, and the consequences for private property [Grunebaum on memory and justice in South Africa](http://www.scielo.org.za/scielo.php?pid=S1947-94172018000200010&script=sci_arttext).

The Direct Action Centre for Peace and Memory emerged as a counter-memory practice. Founded in 1998 by former freedom fighters and activists, it responded to the limits and silences of the TRC. Until it closed in 2008, its Cape Town “Journeys of Remembrance” used streets, squares, and pavements as sites of narrative, movement, and dialogue. Participants co-created knowledge by connecting urban space to experiences of struggle and repression.

A 2021 settler-colonial analysis of the TRC Report describes its treatment of settler colonialism as “ambivalent denial”: the report acknowledges colonial structures while also producing denials that enable settler innocence and democracy without decolonization [analysis of the TRC through a settler-colonial lens](https://doi.org/10.1177/09646639211022786). This perspective does not deny the Commission’s importance. It shows that reconciliation can be both a genuine opening and a mechanism for managing the limits of political change.

### Feminist and queer counter-memory

Gendered reclamation reveals how public monuments can reproduce the exclusions of the historiography they claim to correct. The Portrait Monument, presented to the United States Congress in February 1921, represented Susan B. Anthony, Elizabeth Cady Stanton, and Lucretia Mott. It was placed in a congressional basement broom closet the day after its inauguration and remained there for 76 years. Its return in 1997 was celebrated as a feminist victory, but Black activists criticized its representation of suffrage as the achievement of three white middle-class women. Delores Tucker and the National Congress of Black Women sought to add Sojourner Truth; the request to modify the original failed, but a separate Truth bust was installed in 2009 [study of feminist monuments](https://www.mdpi.com/2409-9252/4/4/23).

The Women’s Rights Pioneers Monument, unveiled in New York’s Central Park in 2020, repeated and revised the problem. The original design placed Stanton and Anthony at a table with a parchment naming other activists. Critics argued that the composition made the two white women appear to write the movement’s history and treated the 19th Amendment of 1920 as the culmination of a struggle that, for many women of color, remained incomplete until the Voting Rights Act of 1965. After criticism, the design removed the parchment and added Sojourner Truth, but a letter signed by approximately 20 mostly African-American activists and academics argued that the final composition falsely implied equal experiences and regular collaboration among the women.

Lisa Tetrault’s scholarship is important here because it links commemoration to historiography. Stanton and Anthony’s multi-volume *History of Woman Suffrage* did not merely record the movement; it sacralized Seneca Falls as its origin and elevated particular leaders. The monument controversy thus concerned not only who appeared in bronze but which earlier historical narrative would be made public. Historiography and commemoration operated reciprocally: scholarship exposed the exclusions embedded in the monument, while the monument made those historiographical debates visible to a broad public.

Queer memorialization similarly reclaims people excluded from national narratives while questioning whether visibility itself guarantees inclusion. Amsterdam’s Homomonument, inaugurated in 1987, consists of three pink granite triangles representing past, present, and future. The pink triangle, originally a Nazi concentration-camp badge for homosexual prisoners, was reappropriated as a symbol of queer pride from the 1970s onward. A 2024 case-study survey of 343 visitors found that the site produces both inclusion and exclusion and sits between older gay memory and newer “post-gay” public memory. The study warns that LGBTQ+ visibility does not automatically create safety or acceptance [study of Amsterdam’s Homomonument](https://doi.org/10.1177/17506980241276426).

The former Uckermark camp offers another example. Approximately 1,200 girls and young women were incarcerated there between 1942 and 1945, many classified by the Nazi state as “asocial.” Unlike nearby Ravensbrück, which became one of East Germany’s national memorial sites, Uckermark was largely forgotten until feminist, lesbian, queer, and trans antifascist activists began organizing in 1997. Their signage, landscaping, mapping, installations, and recurring memorial events constitute what Luhmann calls “memory care work.” The practice produces “queer akinship”: relations across generations that connect activists to remembered victims without collapsing their different experiences [Luhmann on Uckermark counter-memorial activism](https://doi.org/10.1177/17506980221142980).

These examples show that counter-memory is not simply a demand for representation. It can also seek different forms: participatory rather than monumental, unfinished rather than conclusive, relational rather than heroic, and attentive to the conditions of present exclusion.

### Dalit, Adivasi, and Muslim histories in India

Indian counter-memory challenges the state’s national narrative through oral history, literature, graphic fiction, digital archives, and personal testimony. A 2026 study of Dalit and Adivasi counter-histories treats oral accounts, folk memory, lived experience, and personal stories as alternative archives against official bureaucratic history. It identifies suffering, hunger, resistance, dignity, and survivance as subjects that dominant history has marginalized [study of Dalit and Adivasi counter-histories](https://doi.org/10.53032/tvcr/2026.v8n2.37).

The comparison of Bama’s *Karukku* and Mahasweta Devi’s *Dust on the Road* shows different forms of counter-memory. Devi’s work emphasizes activist documentation, collective suffering, and political resistance; Bama’s emphasizes personal testimony, memory, and spiritual questioning. Both move historical authority away from state archives and toward embodied experience.

Graphic fiction performs a similar intervention in Muslim histories. Singh’s study of post-2014 Indian graphic narratives describes them as a resistant archive that replaces stock images of Muslims as villains or victims with accounts of ordinary life and agency. In *Shaheen Bagh: A Graphic Recollection*, Muslim women appear as mothers, workers, neighbors, and protesters. In *Munnu: A Boy from Kashmir*, visual metaphors portray Kashmiri Muslim identity as precious and precarious rather than reducing it to familiar religious stereotypes [Singh on Indian Muslim graphic narratives](https://doi.org/10.36993/rjoe.2024.9.1.706).

These forms have limits. The graphic-fiction corpus is in English and tends toward urban, educated, and sometimes global audiences. The study contains no audience-reception data, so claims about persuasive effect are interpretations of textual and visual form rather than measured outcomes. Parandhama likewise reports that digital archives, historian webinars, student groups, and organizations such as Karwaan have not achieved the institutional reach or statewide readership of official textbooks.

The strongest evidence that historical representation can alter social attitudes comes from a preregistered experiment with 1,592 respondents in India. Participants were randomly assigned inclusive, exclusive, or baseline historical exercises based on school-textbook material. Inclusive representations increased Muslim participants’ perceived centrality, leadership aspirations, entitlement, and support for Muslim politicians; exclusive representations increased Hindu participants’ perceived centrality. Yet Hindu respondents were largely unmoved in their demand for Muslim leaders. The result is both hopeful and cautionary: inclusive history can strengthen minority agency, but changing majority perceptions may be more difficult [experimental study of historical representation and leadership](https://doi.org/10.1017/s000305542300117x).

## 5. Commemorative Practices and the Shaping of Historiography

Commemoration is often treated as the public expression of a history already established by scholars. In practice, monuments, museums, anniversaries, rituals, textbooks, and memorial sites help determine which questions historians ask, which sources receive attention, and which identities appear historically central.

### Monuments as contested narratives

A monument is not meaningful only because of its material durability. A 2026 review of monuments and politics defines monumentality through the way a place is used to form layered communal narratives over time. Meanings accumulate as political orders change. A statue can continue to function as a site of memory after its removal because the empty pedestal, photographs, controversy, and legal dispute preserve the earlier symbolic conflict [Annual Review of Political Science on monuments](https://www.annualreviews.org/content/journals/10.1146/annurev-polisci-042224-082158).

Confederate monuments in the United States show how public memory can outlive the period it claims to represent. Lost Cause ideology recast the Confederacy’s defeat as noble and shifted attention from slavery and institutionalized violence to states’ rights, constitutionalism, and a chivalric past. Monuments, textbooks, and historic sites circulated this interpretation. Many monuments were erected during periods of Jim Crow and white political consolidation, not immediately after the Civil War [summary of Lost Cause and Confederate-monument scholarship](https://cdr.lib.unc.edu/downloads/gb19fc176).

The meaning of these monuments changed as racial politics changed. The massacre of nine African-American worshippers at Mother Emanuel Church in Charleston on June 17, 2015, and the white supremacist rally in Charlottesville on August 12, 2017, intensified demands for removal. In Richmond, Virginia, Monument Avenue had developed between 1890 and 1925 as a major Confederate landscape. After George Floyd’s death in 2020, Lee’s statue became a surface for projections of George Floyd, Malcolm X, and Angela Davis, as well as performances by racial-justice activists. The site temporarily became a counter-memory stage before Lee and other Confederate statues were removed in 2021 [study of feminist and public monuments in the United States](https://www.mdpi.com/2076-0787/13/6/153).

A national dataset of 1,800 Confederate monuments shows that removal is shaped by local political and institutional context. Benjamin and colleagues estimate that a county’s Democratic vote share was associated with a 27-percentage-point higher likelihood of removal. State restrictions were associated with a 10-percentage-point lower likelihood. Of 130 monuments removed by August 21, 2018, 82—63 percent—were in states without legislation restricting dismantling. The researchers also found that a larger African-American population was associated with a 41-percentage-point decrease in removal likelihood, while the interaction between a substantial Black population and an NAACP chapter was associated with a 34-percentage-point increase. These are statistical associations from a logistic-regression analysis, not proof that any single political factor mechanically caused a removal [Benjamin and colleagues on Confederate monuments](https://doi.org/10.1017/s1049096519002026).

The public did not divide simply between preservation and removal. A 2019 Elon Poll reported that 65.3 percent of North Carolina respondents—955 people—favored keeping Confederate monuments in public spaces, while 34.7 percent—507 people—favored removal. At the same time, 72.7 percent considered contextual plaques a good idea. The figures suggest that the dispute concerns not only whether a monument remains but what kind of authority its continued presence communicates.

The alternatives can be compared directly:

| Intervention | Example | Historical effect | Main limitation |
|---|---|---|---|
| Removal and relocation | Lexington, Kentucky, 2018 | Moved two Confederate statues from a prominent site near a former slave market to a less prominent private cemetery | Cooperation can reduce conflict but does not settle the meaning of the objects |
| Contextualization | Forsyth Park, Savannah, 2018 | Renamed a “Confederate Monument” as a “Civil War Memorial” and added a plaque acknowledging its Confederate origin | Critics argue that text may not counteract a large visual symbol |
| Artistic reoccupation | Richmond, 2020–2021 | Turned a Confederate site into a platform for projections, performance, graffiti, and racial-justice messages | Temporary interventions may disappear unless institutions preserve them |
| Deliberate absence | Baltimore proposals | Empty pedestals and a possible Harriet Tubman rededication would make removal itself part of the story | The proposal was not reported as a completed outcome |

Lexington is significant because the removal and relocation of two statues in 2018 did not become a focus of violent regional or national controversy. The Annual Review attributes this partly to years of communication and cooperation among civic leaders and community groups. Savannah pursued contextualization: a plaque stated that the monument was erected in 1875 to Confederate dead, redesigned in 1879, and rededicated in 2018 to all Civil War dead. The case is often presented as a successful reduction of protest, but cited scholars question whether adjacent text can neutralize the visual dominance of a monument.

Baltimore offers a different possibility. After statues were removed, empty pedestals remained at three sites. One proposal suggested plaques explaining what had been removed and why, while a grove could be rededicated to Harriet Tubman. Here absence becomes a historical object. The removal does not erase the past; it makes the prior hierarchy visible and links the site to continuing struggles over freedom and justice [discussion of Baltimore’s empty pedestals](https://www.mdpi.com/2076-0787/13/6/153).

### The contested effects of removal

Scholarly research disagrees about the social effects of monuments. A 2025 American Political Science Review article develops a theory of political symbols as common-knowledge signals of social order. Its historical analysis of counties in the eleven former Confederate states between 1877 and 1928 finds that counties where Confederate monuments were built were less likely to experience lynchings or public executions. The study estimates that approximately 315 of 3,090 lynchings and 725 of 5,433 performative-violence events did not occur because of monument presence, implying a 10–13 percent reduction. The proposed mechanism is not that monuments were benign, but that public symbols of white supremacy communicated hierarchy and reduced the need for performative violence by making domination visible.

This finding conflicts with earlier research by Bazzi and colleagues and Henderson and colleagues, which associated monument presence with greater anti-Black sentiment and violence. The 2025 article also finds that, in present-day county analysis, monument removals were associated with more anti-Black hate crimes, but not with antisemitic hate crimes, which it uses as a placebo comparison [American Political Science Review on political symbols and monuments](https://doi.org/10.1017/s0003055425101007).

The disagreement illustrates why monuments cannot be interpreted through symbolism alone. One study measures the historical relationship between monument presence and public violence; another links monuments to attitudes and violence; a third examines removal and contemporary hate crimes. The periods, outcomes, causal assumptions, and mechanisms differ. A monument can simultaneously communicate racial domination, provoke resistance, stabilize a social order for some people, and threaten the status of others. Removal can be justice-oriented recontextualization and a signal of contested status. No single estimate resolves the political or ethical question of what a community should do with the site.

### Museums and memorial sites

Museums make interpretation visible through architecture, sequencing, labels, lighting, objects, and the movement of visitors. The Terror House museum connects fascist and communist violence through a building used by both regimes, but its disproportionate attention to communism and its contemporary “wall of perpetrators” make the museum an ideological intervention in current Hungarian politics. Auschwitz, by contrast, has shifted from state-socialist preservation to a human-rights frame, demonstrating that even a site associated with an apparently universal crime is continually reinterpreted.

Memorial sites can also reveal layers that official design conceals. Research on colonial monuments in Germany examines the Pogge bust in Rostock, the Bremen elephant, and sites in Berlin where colonialism, National Socialism, and the German Democratic Republic overlap. The argument is that existing memorials often fail to show how successive actors attached different meanings to the same site. Redesigning them to expose those layers would make memory politics itself part of public history [study of colonial memorial sites in Germany](https://refubium.fu-berlin.de/handle/fub188/48779?locale-attribute=en).

Bears Ears National Monument in Utah demonstrates how legal designation can reinterpret Indigenous history while remaining politically reversible. President Barack Obama’s 2016 proclamation recognized archaeological, artistic, historical, religious, and spiritual significance to the Ute Mountain Ute, Navajo, Ute, Hopi, and Zuni peoples. President Donald Trump reduced the monument’s size and scope; President Joe Biden largely restored it in 2021. The legal status of the landscape therefore became a struggle over which historical and spiritual meanings the state would protect [Annual Review of Political Science on Bears Ears](https://www.annualreviews.org/content/journals/10.1146/annurev-polisci-042224-082158).

Visitor research complicates the assumption that museum interpretation changes beliefs. The study summarized in the *Humanities* article reports that visitors often interpret historical sites through prior identity, knowledge, and bias and may ignore information that conflicts with existing commitments. Yet emotionally connective and interactive exhibits can create openings for perspective-taking. The Immigration Museum of Melbourne’s simulation of a hate-speech incident on a tram is presented as an example of how affect and participation may engage visitors more effectively than abstract information. This remains a possibility, not proof that any particular exhibit changes attitudes.

### Rituals, anniversaries, and repetition

Commemorative rituals produce authority through repetition. A fixed date makes a complex process appear to have a single beginning or climax. Trouillot’s analysis of Columbus shows how October 12 became a repository for a narrative that did not exist in that form in 1492. The 1892 Spanish quadricentennial linked Columbus to national revitalization, diplomatic influence, and imperial nostalgia; the Chicago World’s Columbian Exposition of 1893 connected him to commercial expansion, U.S. exceptionalism, and the political economy of the hemisphere. The 1992 quincentennial exposed the fragility of this apparent consensus because Indigenous, Black, Latin American, Caribbean, and Jewish voices contested the celebratory script [Trouillot, *Silencing the Past*](https://www.metodos.work/wp-content/uploads/2021/05/Michel-Rolph-Trouillot-Silencing-the-Past_-Power-and-the-Production-of-History-20th-Anniversary.pdf).

Russia’s Victory Day, Defender of the Fatherland Day, Russia Day, and National Unity Day perform similar work in a different political context. A 2026 study of Telegram posts by 20 nationalist actors alongside official speeches and ministry material from February 2022 to February 2026 finds that these holidays are “unstable signifiers.” They do not transmit one stable collective memory or function as simple instruments of state propaganda. They reveal competition over Russian identity, Soviet continuity, and the meaning of the war [study of Russian national holidays](https://lup.lub.lu.se/student-papers/record/9238467/file/9238474.pdf).

The observation is important because ritual repetition does not guarantee interpretive unity. Public ceremonies can stabilize a national story, but they can also expose disagreement among state institutions, political movements, families, veterans, minorities, and local communities.

### Textbooks and the feedback into historiography

Textbooks are particularly influential because they turn historiography into a routine experience of childhood. Their selection of chapters, maps, images, names, and causal explanations helps define what a nation is and which groups count as historical protagonists.

Indian textbook conflicts show how political change feeds back into historical writing. NCERT revisions have altered the balance between ancient, medieval, colonial, and contemporary history. Russia’s single cultural standard and Ukraine’s competing national curricula likewise transform scholarly disputes over Kyivan Rus, the Holodomor, the Second World War, the OUN and UPA, and the Soviet period into standardized public knowledge.

Textbooks can also teach geography as history. A comparison of Indian and Pakistani high-school textbooks found that students living perhaps no more than 50 miles apart, whose grandparents may have lived as neighbors, are taught to imagine themselves as inheritors of different pasts and inhabitants of different geographical spaces. Indian textbooks use colonial-era cartography to present India’s boundaries as natural and treat external influences as foreign; Pakistani textbooks underplay subcontinental connections and emphasize affinities with the Islamic world [Joshi on Indian and Pakistani textbooks](https://doi.org/10.1080/19472498.2010.485379).

The feedback into historiography operates in both directions. Historians produce textbooks, but curricula also establish the questions that later generations of historians regard as central. If a community’s experience is absent from the school narrative, fewer students encounter it as a legitimate field of inquiry. If a state-funded museum or institute elevates a theme, it can direct research grants, archival access, public attention, and professional careers toward that theme.

## 6. How Historical Memory Serves Current Agendas

### Identity and belonging

Historical memory helps define the boundaries of the political community. Russia’s claim that Russians and Ukrainians share one indivisible historical people denies Ukrainian sovereignty at the level of historical identity. Ukraine’s counter-narrative defines sovereignty through separation from imperial domination. India’s Hindutva narrative presents Hindu civilization as the authentic core of the nation and Muslims as an interruption or threat. Poland’s mnemonic populism defines proper citizenship through national innocence and resistance to foreign accusation.

The Indian experiment with inclusive history provides unusually direct evidence that historical representation can affect perceptions of belonging. Inclusive narratives increased Muslims’ perceived centrality and leadership aspirations. The result confirms a central theoretical claim: historical representation is not merely descriptive. It affects who feels entitled to speak for the nation and who is treated as entitled to lead. But the relative immobility of Hindu respondents shows that changing minority self-perception is easier than changing majority willingness to share national authority.

Feminist and queer memorials reveal the same process at a different scale. When women, queer people, or racialized minorities appear as historical subjects rather than allegories, public space communicates that they are part of the political “we.” Yet a small number of celebrated figures can create a new hierarchy. Sojourner Truth, Harriet Tubman, and Ida B. Wells are repeatedly used to represent Black women’s activism, while the collective labor of thousands of less famous women remains less visible. Inclusion can therefore reproduce a politics of exemplary individuals rather than a history of movements.

### Legitimacy and state authority

States use historical memory to legitimate institutions, laws, and political leaders. The EU’s Holocaust narrative, in Stenlund’s analysis, provides a moral foundation for legislation against hate speech and for constitutional supremacy. Russia’s constitutional amendments used ancestral and religious language to support the extension of presidential tenure. Poland’s Holocaust law presented the state as guardian of national honor. Ukraine’s decommunization laws presented the state as the protector of a sovereign national history.

Memory laws are especially significant because they convert interpretation into obligation. Nekoliak distinguishes non-punitive laws—commemorative designations, victim status, and parliamentary resolutions—from punitive laws that ban public discourse and impose criminal or administrative sanctions. Bucholc similarly distinguishes a law criminalizing Holocaust denial, which regulates historical views, from a lustration law, which targets people rather than interpretations.

The legitimacy gained through legal remembrance is unstable.
